title: audit-painting-auth-review-fixes
assumedKnowledge: You have worked on the painting app: a Deno server over Turso SQLite, passkey sign-in with signed cookies, and a browser client that keeps strokes in IndexedDB and pushes them through an outbox.

concepts.title: Session epoch is the only revocation lever
concepts.statement: Say why bumping session_epoch is the one way the app can end a signed cookie, and what has to happen for the bump to reach a device that is still writing.

options.text: The profile's session_epoch is bumped, so every cookie minted before it fails its next assertion.
The acting device's cookie is re-minted at the new epoch, so the device that asked stays signed in.
The ensuredProfiles memo expires after 30 seconds, so the caller's profile row is read again.

misconceptions.statement: Revoking a session only affects the device that made the request.
Letting a cached profile row expire is what signs the other devices out.
An epoch bump signs out every device, including the one that requested it.

cards.heading: A primitive nobody calls is not a mechanism
body: Before the auth review, the painting app had no way at all to invalidate a session. The cookie is the session: there is no server-side session table to delete a row from, and the cookie carried a 400-day max-age. The one lever that existed, session_epoch, was carried in the token format and asserted by twelve mutating routes, and bumpSessionEpoch() even had a doc comment calling itself the sign-out-everywhere primitive. Nothing outside a test ever called it.

The fix wires the primitive to two events. Removing a passkey bumps the profile's epoch, and POST /api/auth/logout/all backs a new Sign out everywhere control. Every cookie minted at the old epoch now fails its next assertion on a mutating route. The device that made the request would be caught too, so the same response re-mints that device's cookie at the new epoch. Revocation is therefore all devices except the one acting, which is exactly what removing a passkey or pressing the control means.

cards.heading: Revocation has to reach the caller it is aimed at
body: Bumping the epoch changes a row in the database. Whether a live caller notices depends on whether the server reads that row again. The routes asserted the epoch against ensuredProfiles, a memo of the profile row that was populated once and kept forever. A device pushing strokes every four seconds hit the memo every time and was never re-checked, so the revocation could not evict the exact caller it was for.

The memo now has a 30 second TTL. A revoked device that keeps writing is accepted for at most 30 seconds after the bump, then its next push re-reads the profile, sees the new epoch and fails. The bound is the price of not reading the profile on every request; thirty seconds is short enough for a stolen device and long enough that the four-second push loop does not turn into a database read per stroke.

concepts.title: A cascade that only ran in the test
concepts.statement: Explain why ON DELETE CASCADE did nothing on a serving connection and how the delete paths remove dependent rows safely without it.

options.text: SQLite's foreign_keys pragma is per connection and off by default, so the declared cascade never fires in serving code.
The migration connection had turned foreign keys on, so the cascade ran there and the test saw it work.
The delete removes canvas_events itself, guarded by EXISTS on the canvas row so a no-match delete cannot gut history.

misconceptions.statement: The cascade test ran on a connection with foreign keys off, the same as production.
Turning the pragma on during migration leaves it on for the serving connections too.
After the fix, the declared cascade is what removes a deleted painting's strokes.

cards.heading: The cascade never reached a serving connection
body: canvas_events declares ON DELETE CASCADE, and the test that covered it passed. It passed on the migration connection, where migrateDatabase() had run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON. That pragma is per connection and off by default, so no serving connection ever had it, and deleting a painting silently kept every stroke. When the review looked, dev held 768 orphaned event rows against 14 live canvases.

The obvious fix, turning the pragma on in createDb(), is not available. getDb() is synchronous across about 60 call sites, so there is no place to await a pragma before the first query, and the fetch-based Turso client can re-establish its stream and drop a per-connection setting without telling anyone. A setting that can quietly revert is not something a delete path can rely on, so the delete paths stopped relying on it.

cards.heading: Delete your own dependents, and guard the delete
body: Each delete path now removes its own canvas_events rows explicitly, in the same request as the canvas delete. The event delete is guarded with EXISTS over the same ownership and state predicate the canvas delete uses, so if the canvas delete matches no row, because the caller does not own it or it is not in the expected state, the event delete matches nothing either. Without the guard, a delete that was refused for the canvas could still gut that canvas's history.

The tests changed to match the world they are meant to describe. They now run with foreign keys explicitly OFF, the way production does, so a future test cannot pass by accident on a connection that happens to enforce the schema. The lesson generalises: a declared constraint is a promise the engine may or may not keep on this connection, and the code that needs the behaviour has to either verify the setting or do the work itself.

concepts.title: Signing out is a teardown, in order
concepts.statement: Order the three steps of sign-out on a shared device and say which cached value was dangerous to leave behind.

options.text: Drain the outbox first, so pending strokes reach the server while a session that can send them still exists.
Revoke on the server before erasing, so a failed revocation leaves a device that can still retry.
Erase localStorage and IndexedDB last, including the cached WebAuthn user.id, so the next profile inherits nothing.

misconceptions.statement: Pending local strokes can be discarded at sign-out because the server already has them.
Replacing the cookie is all a sign-out needs to do.
Local painting state is scoped to the profile, so it cannot leak to the next user of the device.

cards.heading: Sign-out replaced the cookie and nothing else
body: Before the fix, signing out swapped the session cookie and stopped. Everything else on the device survived: the outbox of strokes not yet pushed, the current canvas id, the local event history and the cached WebAuthn user record. On a shared device that is a hand-over, not a sign-out.

Sign-out is now a teardown with a fixed order. First the outbox is drained, because pending strokes can only be sent by a session that still exists; once the cookie is gone they are unsendable. Then the server is asked to revoke, so that if the revocation fails the device still has a session to retry with. Only then is local state erased. When the drain cannot save some work, the app asks rather than discarding it, because the person signing out may not know they had unsaved strokes at all.

cards.heading: Unscoped local state becomes the next user's state
body: Nothing in localStorage or IndexedDB is scoped by profile, and it cannot be: the client is never told an owner id. So the next person on the device inherited the previous profile's currentCanvasId and local history, which sync.js renders before it has asked the server anything. The stale cached WebAuthn user.id was worse than stale. When the next profile renamed its handle, the rename relabelled the signed-out account's passkey in the platform password manager.

The same unscoped state broke keep-this-device's-draft. The client trusted the canvas id it asked for instead of the id the server granted, which is fine while they match and wrong precisely after a sign-out with local work on it, when the requested id belongs to another profile. The editor pointed at a canvas the profile did not own and drained into a 403 forever. It now honours acceptedPreferredId and re-keys pending events onto the granted draft.

questions.stem: A user of the painting app removes one of their passkeys. Apart from deleting the credential row, what does the server do to the profile's sessions on other devices?

feedback.bump: Right. There is no session row to delete; the epoch is the only thing every cookie is checked against.
feedback.remint: Re-minting is what keeps the acting device signed in. It is a consequence of the bump, not the revocation itself.
feedback.recheck: The memo TTL only controls how quickly a device notices; it does not end any session on its own.

questions.stem: Sign out everywhere is pressed on a laptop. The bump would invalidate the laptop's own cookie too. What stops the laptop from being signed out by the request it just sent?

feedback.remint: Right. The same response sets a fresh cookie carrying the new epoch, so only the other devices fail.
feedback.bump: The bump is what would sign the laptop out. Something in the same response has to undo that for the acting device.
feedback.recheck: The memo affects when the server re-reads the profile, not which cookie the laptop holds.

questions.stem: After Sign out everywhere, a revoked tablet keeps pushing strokes every four seconds. Because of the ensuredProfiles memo it is still accepted for a bounded time. What is that bound, in seconds?
questions.feedback: About 30 seconds, the memo's TTL. The first push after the memo expires re-reads the profile and fails the epoch assertion.

questions.stem: Which POST route backs the Sign out everywhere control in the painting app?
questions.feedback: POST /api/auth/logout/all. It bumps the epoch and re-mints the acting device's cookie in the same response.

questions.stem: A tablet was revoked a moment ago and keeps pushing strokes every four seconds. What eventually makes the server notice the new epoch for that tablet?

feedback.recheck: Right. Until the memo expires the server compares the tablet's cookie against a stale profile row.
feedback.bump: The bump already happened. The question is why the tablet is still accepted for a while afterwards.
feedback.remint: Only the device that made the revoking request gets a new cookie. The tablet keeps its old one.

questions.stem: canvas_events declares ON DELETE CASCADE, yet deleting a painting in dev left hundreds of stroke rows behind. Why did the cascade not run?

feedback.pragma: Right. A declared cascade is enforced only on a connection that has foreign_keys on, and serving connections never did.
feedback.migration: The migration connection did have it on, which is why the test passed. That setting never reached the serving connections.
feedback.exists: The EXISTS-guarded delete is the fix. It explains how strokes are removed now, not why the cascade failed.

questions.stem: The test covering the canvas_events cascade passed before the fix, while production kept every orphaned stroke. Why did the test pass?

feedback.migration: Right. migrateDatabase() had run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on the very connection the test then used.
feedback.pragma: That is why production failed. The test connection was different: it had foreign keys on.
feedback.exists: The guarded delete did not exist yet when the test passed.

questions.stem: Which SQLite pragma must be ON for a declared ON DELETE CASCADE to fire on a connection?
questions.feedback: foreign_keys. It is per connection and off by default, which is the whole story of this Concept.

questions.stem: A request deletes a painting the caller does not own, so the canvas delete matches no row. After the fix, what stops the request from removing that painting's stroke history anyway?

feedback.exists: Right. The event delete repeats the canvas predicate inside EXISTS, so it matches nothing when the canvas delete matches nothing.
feedback.pragma: The pragma being off is why the cascade cannot be relied on. It does not protect anything by itself.
feedback.migration: The migration connection is not the one serving this request.

questions.stem: Sign-out in the painting app is three steps in a fixed order. Which step happens first, and why must it?

feedback.drain: Right. Once the session is revoked the pending strokes have no way to reach the server.
feedback.revoke: Revoking first would strand every stroke still in the outbox.
feedback.erase: Erasing first would destroy the outbox before anything in it was sent.

questions.stem: The outbox has been drained and the server has been asked to revoke the session. Why does the app revoke before it erases local state, rather than after?

feedback.revoke: Right. If revocation fails, a device with its state intact can retry; a device already wiped cannot.
feedback.drain: The drain is already done at this point. The question is about the order of the last two steps.
feedback.erase: Erasing first would leave a device with no session to retry the revocation with.

questions.stem: The client asked to keep a device draft under a preferred canvas id, but the server granted a different one. Which response field names the canvas the editor must now use and re-key its pending events onto?
questions.feedback: acceptedPreferredId. Trusting the requested id instead pointed the editor at another profile's canvas and drained into a 403 forever.

questions.stem: After a sign-out on a shared device, the next profile renamed its handle and the rename relabelled the signed-out account's passkey in the platform password manager. Which sign-out step now prevents that?

feedback.erase: Right. The cached WebAuthn user.id is local state, and only erasing it stops the next profile from reusing it.
feedback.drain: Draining sends strokes; it does not touch the cached WebAuthn user record.
feedback.revoke: Server-side revocation cannot reach a value cached in the browser.

sources.title: fix: close the session-revocation, deletion, and sign-out gaps found in an auth review
